10340-dab-kinzer-a-story-of-a-growing-bo:
William O. Stoddard published this boys' story in 1884, following Dab Kinzer on a Long Island farm and coast. Dab starts with a new suit and a wedding, then meets city boys, pigs, boats, and a railway train in a string of comic mishaps. The book treats boyhood as a mix of work, play, and growing sense.

Crabs, a boat wreck, a rescue, fishing, fog, and a cruise in the Swallow fill later chapters. Dab learns to tell one kind of boy from another, and to stand his ground. Readers get a cheerful, old-fashioned tale of farm life, seaside fun, and a boy becoming steady and kind.
10724-the-store-boy:
Horatio Alger Jr. wrote The Store Boy in his familiar rags-to-respectability manner, following Ben Barclay, a country lad on the road. The story opens as Ben, driving a horse, meets a hard-looking tramp who begs a ride to Pentonville. Ben hesitates, wary of so rough a traveling companion, before the journey begins.

From that meeting, Alger builds a tale of work, honesty, and pluck, as Ben seeks a place in a store and proves his worth. The novel belongs to Alger's long run of boys' books that sold by the million. Young readers get adventure with a moral, in the style that made Alger's name a byword for rising by merit.
12493-how-john-became-a-man-life-story-o:
Isabel C. Byrum's little volume tells the true life story of John, a motherless boy, as a moral lesson for young readers. Her preface hopes the book will show boys the wrong in evil habits. It quotes that a people are destroyed for lack of knowledge, and trusts John's earnest prayer that his story may help others escape snares.

John's path runs from temptation and harmful habit toward prayer, discipline and manhood, told in simple, earnest prose. Illustrations, including one captioned Learning to Pray, reinforce the lesson. The book belongs to early twentieth-century uplift literature for boys, direct in aim and plain in style, valuing character over adventure.
12633-a-happy-boy:
Bjørnstjerne Bjørnson's Happy Boy, translated from the Norse by Rasmus B. Anderson in an author's edition, was written in 1859 and 1860. Anderson, designated by Bjørnson as his American translator, cooperated with the author, who revised each work before translation, giving personal attention to the edition.

A preface calls the tale Bjørnson's best story of peasant life, praising distinct characters, profound psychological insight, artless simplicity and thorough sympathy with hero and surroundings. Popular throughout Scandinavia, the story follows a Norwegian farm boy toward happiness through work, love and faith. The book offers a gentle, classic tale of rural Norway, in a translation the author himself approved.
14533-hocken-and-hunken-a-tale-of-troy:
Arthur Thomas Quiller-Couch, writing as Q, set this Cornish tale in Troy, a small port town of sailors, barbers, and farmers. Captain Cai Hocken hauls ashore to open the story.

Cai and his friend 'Bias, both elderly bachelors, fall for the widow Mrs. Bosenna, and their rivalry runs through regattas, parlour games, letters, auctions, and a final jubilee. Quiller-Couch writes in warm dialect and gentle comedy. The novel is a charming tale of late love in a Cornish town, full of boats, gossip, and second chances. Q's Troy stories were beloved by Cornish readers.
16682-adrien-leroy:
Charles Garvice wrote this London tale of clubs, dinners, and high society, issued by George Newnes in London. It opens on a cold spring night in the West End, where shops shut, tired workers head home, and rich folk in taxis speed west for dinner. Two men in evening dress wait at a Pall Mall club for Standon and Leroy.

Garvice sets rich life against work life in the first pages, then lets love and social games take over. The tale moves through clubs, drawing rooms, and late dinners, with talk as its main engine. Readers who like old society novels will find a smooth, talky romance of London's smart set and the hearts caught in it.
16867-the-adventures-of-odysseus-and-the:
Padraic Colum wrote this 1918 retelling of Odysseus and the tale of Troy, issued by Macmillan in New York with pictures by Willy Pogany. Colum dedicated it to Hughie and Peter, whose imaginations rise to deeds and wonders. Part one follows Telemachus seeking his father and hearing the tale of Troy from Menelaus and Helen. Part two follows Odysseus leaving Calypso's isle, meeting the Phaeacians, and telling of Cyclopes, Scylla, and Charybdis.

Colum retells Homer in clear, storyteller prose for young readers, keeping wonder and peril in fair share. His book has stayed a favorite first Odyssey, reprinted many times through the 1920s. Young readers get a grand, readable voyage home, best read before tackling Homer's epic in full.
16990-the-story-of-troy:
M. Clarke wrote this 1897 school book on the story of Troy. The American Book Company issued it in New York, Cincinnati, and Chicago. A head of Homer from the British Museum serves as frontispiece. Contents run from Homer, father of poetry, and the gods into Troy before the siege. The judgment of Paris, the league against Troy, and the wrath of Achilles follow. The death of Hector and the fall of Troy come next. The Greek chiefs after the war close the book.

Clarke retells the Iliad in plain, schoolroom prose, with chapters that track the war year by year. The book gives young readers a clear first Troy, without the full epic's weight. It still serves as a friendly introduction to Homer's tale, best read before tackling the Iliad itself.
18646-gypsy-s-cousin-joy:
Elizabeth Stuart Phelps wrote this Gypsy book, reissued at New York in 1895 by Dodd, Mead and Company, with a new preface by the author. Gypsy is a lively tomboy in short dresses and long stockings who paddles rafts, climbs trees, skates, and tramps, usually muddy and a little torn. Phelps, who wrote the tales when hardly more than a girl herself, marvels in the preface that Gypsy is now thirty years old in print.

This volume brings cousin Joy into Gypsy's circle, with chapters on news, chestnuts, a discovery, a night's story, and a climb up Rattlesnake. Fun, health, hope, truth, and kindness mark the heroine throughout. The book remains a cheerful classic of girls' fiction from the 1800s.
1948-the-story-of-a-bad-boy:
Thomas Bailey Aldrich's Story of a Bad Boy follows Tom Bailey, a boy sent from New Orleans to live with his grandfather in Rivermouth, New Hampshire, and to attend school there. Tom's badness is of the mild, boyish kind: pranks, scrapes, and adventures with his friends, told by Tom himself in later years.

The book is often called the first American boys' novel. Its charm lies in its realism: a boy who is neither saint nor villain, in a town drawn from Aldrich's own childhood. Readers who know Tom Sawyer will see the debt, and readers new to Aldrich will find a sunny, funny introduction to a New England boyhood.
19751-the-mayor-of-troy:
Arthur Thomas Quiller-Couch wrote this comic novel of Troy, a Cornish borough, published in the early nineteen hundreds and dedicated to Kenneth Grahame and the crew of a small ship. A major, a mayor, a millennium, and a battle of gallants and diehards drive the fun.

Chapters run from a Guernsey merchant's meddling to a bomb, a farewell to Albion, and a merry-go-round close, with the major learning that no man is necessary. Quiller-Couch's Troy books blend Cornish local life with high-spirited farce. Later chapters stage the battle of Talland Cove, where Gunner Sobey takes his turn.
19999-the-drummer-boy:
Mary Anna Phinney's The Drummer Boy is a story of the Civil War. In 1861 the Manly family gathers in their little sitting room. A question of the most serious importance faces them all. It concerns Frank in particular, the drummer boy of the title. Frank's mother sits by the table, pretending to sew. The family's debate is whether a boy shall march to war. Drummer boys were the army's youngest soldiers.

Thousands of boys under eighteen served as drummers and musicians. Their stories filled Northern magazines during and after the war. Phinney writes Frank's choice with a mother's-eye sympathy. The sitting-room scene weighs duty against a child's safety. Such tales taught young readers the war's cost at home. This one is tender, patriotic period fiction.
20492-terry-or-she-ought-to-have-been-a-:
Terry, or She Ought to Have Been a Boy is a story about a girl with a boy's name and a boy's spirit. A servant in the house speaks her mind about the christening. Except for that, she tells the mother, the child was born all right.

When you put a man's name on her, the woman says, something got into the poor lamb. That something will take a good while to work out of her. The tale follows Terry's scrapes and high spirits, and it lets readers judge whether a tomboy's ways are a fault at all.
21371-our-soldier-boy:
A British merchant family in Portugal leaves its eight-year-old son with the servants for a few minutes. They are unaware how close the Peninsular War fighting has come. French troops attack, kill the servants, and leave the child with a bad head wound. A corporal of the Fusiliers later finds him while scouting the villa for food.

George Manville Fenn makes the boy the regiment's mascot, raised by the corporal and his wife, with no memory of his real parents. In time he heroically rescues the colonel himself in battle. Months later the Portuguese give a ball for the British victory, and among the guests are the Trevors, whose name belongs to his lost life.
21626-adrift-in-the-wilds-or-the-adventu:
A steamer runs up the California coast at the start of Edward S. Ellis's Adrift in the Wilds, copyrighted in 1887. She is a day's sail from San Francisco, and passengers pack for landing. A money panic back east has ruined Brandon, Herman and Company, driving the tale's start.

Two boys are shipwrecked on the wild shore, far from the golden gate. Tim, their Irish companion, spies Indigenous folk with a cry for heaven to preserve them. A tiny canoe drawn from hiding gives the party a chance. Ellis, a giant of the dime novel, packs peril into every chapter.
21812-paul-gerrard-the-cabin-boy:
Paul Gerrard goes to sea as a cabin boy in this tale by W. H. G. Kingston, a master of boys' sea stories. Paul's father has lost his estates in a legal fight with the Devereux family, and the sea offers the boy a living. To his surprise, a young Devereux serves in the same midshipmen's mess. Paul saves the wounded man's life, and wary dislike slowly turns to friendship.

The tale opens in a Channel gale, with a fine frigate fighting out to open ocean. Kingston fills his pages with swimming, sharks, wrecks, battles, and pirates in his true style. The editor of this edition calls it a cracking audiobook. Young readers get honor, danger, and forgiveness at sea.
22407-the-adventures-of-piang-the-moro-j:
Florence Partello Stuart wrote The Adventures of Piang, the Moro Jungle Boy, in 1917. Piang is a boy of the Moro people in the Philippines. Stuart wrote after finding Americans ignorant of their own colonies.

The general impression, she says, was that Manila was the Philippines. Few knew the group holds several thousand little islands. Each island harbors its distinct tribe, dialect, and religion. Stuart aimed her boy's adventures against that ignorance. Piang's jungle life introduces young readers to Moro country. The book mixes adventure with geography and custom. It shows how American children's books taught empire through one boy's story.
22497-cab-and-caboose-the-story-of-a-rai:
Kirk Munroe wrote Cab and Caboose, the story of a railroad boy. Munroe wrote adventure books that aimed to teach as they thrilled. A later framing note praises wholesome reading for boys' leisure hours.

Boy Scout leaders, that note says, learned a boy must be influenced wisely. His out-of-door life alone would not shape him fully. The diversions of his other leisure moments mattered just as much. Good stories were part of that shaping by design. Within the tale, a boy learns railroading from cab to caboose. Munroe fills the run with signals, yards, and danger. Readers get period railroad life through a young worker's training.
22944-the-history-of-little-peter-the-sh:
Old Betsy walks half a mile each day in The History of Little Peter, the Ship-Boy. She had known Mary Gray from childhood and came daily, without fee or reward, to help during the long illness from which Mary suffered. Peter, meanwhile, spent his days out on the downs, minding Farmer Ashton's flock of sheep.

From such humble beginnings the tale sends its boy toward the sea promised by the title. Peter's story follows the pattern of the improving children's book, hardship, kindness, and reward in steady sequence. The village scenes ground the adventure in real poverty and real charity. Readers meet a vanished England of downs, farms, and sickrooms, drawn by a writer who expected young readers to feel, as well as follow, the plot.
23375-jack-at-sea-all-work-and-no-play-m:
George Manville Fenn wrote this sea tale about Jack, a clever, bookish boy who takes little sport or exercise. His father, Sir John, and the family doctor fret over it. They decide the cure is a voyage. Sir John buys a yacht fit to sail round the world, and the whole party sets off, with Ned, a servant from home, aboard.

Crew, sails, strange ports, and scrapes at sea fill the pages, as Jack learns the world outside his books. The copy used here lacks two pages and part of two more, torn or lost, but the tale runs clear around those gaps. Fenn makes the moral light and the fun broad, showing how work, play, and sea air can turn a dull boy into a livelier one.
23771-the-hoosier-school-boy:
Edward Eggleston published The Hoosier School-Boy in 1883, a school story of Indiana boyhood. Its hero, Jack, arrives as the new scholar and soon earns his place among boys with nicknames like King Milkmaid and Little Christopher Columbus. The frontispiece warns, Not there, not there, my child.

Chapters bring a battle, hat-ball and bull-pen, pigeon pot-pie, and an exploring expedition. Jack defends his friends, chases a fox, and faces being called to account, with a foot-race for money and a spelling lesson along the way. Eggleston, who knew the Hoosier schoolroom from life, writes its rough fun and rough justice with warmth.
24013-the-telegraph-boy:
Horatio Alger Jr. published The Telegraph Boy as the completion of his sketches of street life in New York, begun eleven years earlier with Ragged Dick. Alger dedicates it to three young friends, Lorin and Beatrice Bernheimer and Florine Arnold, and writes with pride of the public's warm reception.

The telegraph boy class, he notes, came into existence only a few years before, yet its boys are already so numerous that scarcely a downtown ride lacks one for a fellow passenger. Most live with parents in comfortable homes, but a few, like his hero, do not. Alger urges readers to help such waifs through the Children's Aid Society, whose wise plans for its young wards had already met abundant success.
24251-left-behind-or-ten-days-a-newsboy:
James Otis, author of Toby Tyler, Mr. Stubbs's Brother, and Raising the Pearl, wrote this boys' book, published by Harper and Brothers in New York as part of Harper's Young People Series, at a dollar a volume. The series beside it offered Captain Polly, Uncle Peter's Trust, Dorymates, The Flamingo Feather, Wakulla, The Ice Queen, and Otis's own Silent Pete and Tim and Tip.

The title gives the plot in brief: a boy left behind spends ten days as a newsboy, learning to fend for himself on city streets. A picture shows a woman feeding him patiently, on page one hundred and twenty. Readers get a plain, kind-hearted story of a boy's short spell of independence, told for young readers.
24663-the-rich-little-poor-boy:
Eleanor Gates, author of The Poor Little Rich Girl, wrote this novel, published at New York and London in 1922. Its chapters are named for a wicked giant, pride and penalty, a feast and an excursion, four millionaires, new friends, and a dearest wish. A picture shows what the boy saw holding him spellbound in his chair.

Gates reverses her earlier tale: here a poor boy finds himself among riches, and must learn what wealth can and cannot give. Her story mixes fantasy, humour, and feeling, with a child's eye for wonder. Young readers get a charming novel about money, wishes, and the things that matter more.
25486-david-the-shepherd-boy:
Amy Steedman retells the boyhood of David for young readers, in Thomas Nelson's Bible story series. David, youngest son of Jesse of Bethlehem, watches his father's flocks on the hillside while seven big brothers do men's work at home. Bethlehem lies off the beaten track, reached by a steep road through olive groves and sheepfields. The boy's days pass among sheep, with only the hills for company.

David's faith proves itself when lion and bear threaten the flock, and he tells Saul that the God who saved him from paw and claws will save him from the Philistine. Saul offers royal armour and sword, but David refuses them, untrained in their use. He takes his shepherd's coat and sling, the only weapon he thoroughly understands. The book pairs David with Joseph the Dreamer and other childhood Bible tales.
26075-the-erie-train-boy:
Horatio Alger Jr.'s 1891 novel follows Fred, a boy working the Erie road, after his father's death leaves his mother and him with far less than they expected. Mr. Ferguson, cold and brief, tells Fred his father failed to insure his life, and the boy must make his own way.

Chapters mix train adventures with a missing valise, a false suspicion that lands Fred in prison, a trap for Mr. Palmer, and calls on Mr. Ferguson and Ruth Patton. Fred falls under suspicion, clears it, and ends a newspaper hero, with Rose Wainwright's party and a run of good luck closing the tale. The book is a straight Alger story of pluck rewarded.
26104-that-scholarship-boy:
Emma Leslie's school story follows the new boy at Torrington's, whose arrival stirs the whole school. Leonard and his sister Duffy puzzle over the stranger's name, while Taylor and his popular party scorn the newcomers as beggars setting themselves up as gentlemen. A quiet combination of students answers the bullying.

The combination's class answers soon show its meaning, and angry Taylor finds the plan backed by parents taken into confidence. Chapters move from brother and sister talk through Dr. Morrison, a champion's stand, and a righteous retribution, ending with news for Mrs. Morrison. The tale rewards pluck, fair play, and loyalty to schoolmates under pressure.
26255-sonny-boy:
Sophie Swett's 1904 children's book follows Sonny Boy Plummer and his six brothers and sisters. It opens with a dinner-table letter from Aunt Kate, the right kind of aunt who never forgets a birthday. Sonny Boy soon goes on a journey, makes friends, and hunts for his white mice, whose loss drives much of the fun.

Later chapters bring a crookeder boy, school days, and a question over who shall be captain of the company. Pictures show Aunt Kate's summons, a coachman clearing the way with his fists, and a boy named Otto at his one good time. Sonny Boy's gift of his mice to Otto mixes joy with grief, and the book praises kindness in a child's plain, warm voice.
27235-the-voyage-alone-in-the-yawl-rob-r:
John MacGregor's The Voyage Alone in the Yawl Rob Roy, sixth edition of 1893 from Sampson Low, logs a lone sail. It runs from London to Paris and by Havre across the Channel to the Isle of Wight. MacGregor, captain of the Royal Canoe Club, cooked and slept on board without any companion.

Fine weather came along the dangerous coast of France, and an amphibious interlude carried the yawl inland to the Paris Exhibition. Across the broad Channel, one hundred miles to Cowes and its regattas, rough water and dark nights of thunder gave way to bright skies on the Thames and Medway.
27666-seek-and-find-or-the-adventures-of:
Oliver Optic, the pen name of William T. Adams, published this boys' story with Lee and Shepard of Boston, entered in 1867 and copyrighted in 1895. It ran third among the serial stories in Our Boys and Girls, as the sequel to Breaking Away.

Optic dedicates the book to his young friend Alice Lee Gookin, and thanks the young friends who wrote hundreds of letters, with generous commendation and an occasional criticism. His hero, Ernest Thornton, is a smart boy, perhaps too smart. His smartness is no worldly cunning, but the stuff of a noble and true man. An illustration shows Ernest swimming for the despatch barrel.
29333-war-letters-of-a-public-school-boy:
Paul Jones, lieutenant of the Tank Corps, wrote the war letters collected in this volume, published by Cassell and Company in 1918 with eight plates. Jones was scholar-elect of Balliol College, Oxford, and leader of the modern side and football captain at Dulwich College in 1914. His father Harry Jones supplies a memoir, calling him the embodiment of the best public-school spirit.

Part one follows Jones from childhood through Dulwich, football, cricket, and editing The Alleynian. Part two prints his war letters, and part three closes the book. A plate shows Rupert Brooke among the illustrations. Readers get a young officer's war in his own words, framed by a father's grief, from the generation that went from school to the trenches.
296-the-cash-boy:
Frank Fowler, a cash boy, learns he is not his mother's son at all. Horatio Alger Jr.'s Cash Boy opens with a conspiracy that stole a baby from his kin and gave him to a kind woman. Mrs. Fowler raises Frank beside her daughter Grace without favor.

At her death Frank learns the truth, and a kind neighbor shelters Grace while Frank sets out to earn his way. Hardship follows, but kindness to an old man reveals his relatives and true name. Alger's moral of honest work carries the tale. The book shows his rags-to-respect formula.
29828-is-he-popenjoy:
Anthony Trollope published Is He Popenjoy? in London in 1879, in a third edition from Chapman and Hall. Life at Manor Cross and the deanery opens the tale, with Lord and Lady George, Miss Mildmay, and Jack de Baron among the early figures. News from Italy, bad tidings, and a visit to Cross Hall gate stir the plot. Then comes the question of chapter fourteen: are we to call him Popenjoy?

The marquis comes home, sees his brother, and moves among his friends, while the claim of the boy from Italy hangs over all. Trollope treats the matter with his usual dry wit and social care. The book is a tale of rank, marriage, and inheritance, where one name can decide a family's fate and fortune.
30463-john-whopper-the-newsboy:
John Whopper, a Boston newsboy, tells tall tales of travel in a book published in 1871 and entered for copyright in 1870. Pictures show his air-line route to China and his visit to the North Pole. He starts one Tuesday morning, very early, carrying a large bundle of papers from Roxbury toward Jamaica Plain.

Hoping to save time, he cuts across rough, barren fields and jumps a fence at a spot he will not name precisely. After about a third of a mile, his shortcut turns strange, and the story launches into comic voyages. Whopper narrates with cheerful exaggeration, turning an ordinary paper round into a globe-spanning joke for young readers.
30567-the-bondboy:
George W. Ogden writes The Bondboy, published in Chicago in October 1922 by A. C. McClurg, following his earlier Trails End, Claim Number One, The Land of Last Chance, and The Rustler of Wind River. Nineteen chapters open with delivered into bondage, a dry-salt man, the spark in the clod, and a stranger at the gate.

Later scenes add the secret of the clover, blood, deliverance, will he tell, and the sealed envelope. Let him hang, Peter's son, the sunbeam on the wall, until the day break, and deserted follow, with the state versus Newbolt near the close. Ogden tells a story of bondage, debt, and a boy's fight for freedom in the American West.
3127-being-a-boy:
Warner calls being a boy one of the best things in the world. It needs no experience, though it takes some practice to be a good one. Its fault is brevity: just as a boy grows used to the state, he must become something else, with far more work and not half so much fun. Yet every boy longs to be a man and chafes at the limits placed on him.

The chapters that follow remember that restless age in detail. Yoking up teams, roaming fields, and dodging chores fill the pages. The book charms because Warner writes as one who has kept the boy's view intact: work is real, play is serious, and growing up looks both welcome and unfair at once.
32246-adventures-and-reminiscences-of-a-:
George T. Ulmer's Adventures and Reminiscences of a Volunteer, or A Drummer Boy from Maine, was entered in 1892. Ulmer served in Company H, Eighth Maine Volunteers, and dedicated the book to the Grand Army of the Republic. Ulmer's preface warns readers plainly. He does not attempt a history of the rebellion, nor assume correctness in dates to a day. He writes with no aim of posing as a hero, since his deeds fell far short of heroism.

Ulmer holds that the war's true heroes mostly died in it. Perhaps writing the book may stamp him a hero, for whose audacity someone may kill him. He intends instead to dress his little work in homely, rugged, everyday language, striving not for literary merit but for a truthful account. Readers get a Civil War drummer boy's memoir, modest, direct, and deliberately unheroic, from a Maine volunteer.
3229-helen-of-troy:
Andrew Lang retells the story of Helen in this 1882 poem, published by George Bell and Sons in London. The Chiswick Press printed it, and an Old French epigraph sets a tone of courtly sorrow before the verse begins. Lang, scholar of myth and ballad, takes the most famous face in Greek story as his subject.

The poem follows Helen from Sparta's court to Troy's walls, weighing beauty, blame, and fate as the old poets weighed them. Lang writes with a classicist's care, in verse that favors music over novelty. Readers who know the Iliad will find a Victorian retelling: respectful of its sources, tender toward its heroine, and aware that no retelling can settle whether Helen chose or was chosen.
33465-little-miss-joy:
Emma Marshall's Little Miss Joy, in a new edition from London in 1892, follows a girl whose story opens with waiting and watching. Its frontispiece shows Patience telling Joy that she has often wished she had known her mother, a tender scene that sets the book's tone. Marshall, author of Little Queenie and Blue Bell, writes for young readers with warmth and moral care.

The tale's charm lies in its gentle, domestic pathos, as Joy learns of her mother and finds her place in a loving home. Its chapters move from waiting to joy itself, with a novelist's eye for a child's heart. For readers who enjoy Victorian girls' books, Little Miss Joy offers a sweet, old-fashioned story of loss, love, and home.
33544-carrots-just-a-little-boy:
Mrs. Molesworth, writing as Ennis Graham, tells the story of a small boy nicknamed Carrots in this 1876 children's book, illustrated by Walter Crane. Thirteen chapters follow Carrots from his sister Floss's baby through his sixth year, his plans, a lost half-sovereign, trouble and recovery, a long-ago story, a bewitched tongue. A little dog named Gip shares his adventures.

Molesworth writes with warmth and humor about a real child's misunderstandings, kindness, and growing sense of right. The book, dedicated to six little cousins, belongs to the best Victorian tradition of family stories, where small domestic events matter greatly. Young readers and adults reading aloud will enjoy its gentle comedy and affectionate tone.
34367-the-last-cruise-of-the-spitfire-or:
The Last Cruise of the Spitfire, or Luke Foster's Strange Voyage, is a boys' sea tale by Edward Stratemeyer, author of Under Dewey at Manila. Lee and Shepard of Boston issued it, with copyrights of 1894 and 1900. It opens the Ship and Shore Series. The preface says the tale tells what befell a boy who ran away from his guardian's home.

Luke Foster could no longer stand the cruel treatment he got there, so the sea took him. Luke tells his own story in his own way. New to the sea, he is carried off on the Spitfire, and his true days on the ocean stand beside what he had fancied sailor life to be. His harsh cousin and dishonest uncle wait in the background of the tale.
35249-a-japanese-boy:
Shiukichi Shigemi tells his own Japanese boyhood in English in a book issued by Henry Holt and Company at New York in 1890. The title page says the book is by himself. Copyright rests with the author in 1889.

His letter to Professor Henry W Farnam owns the faults first. The sketches are rambling, incoherent, and extremely meagre, he says, but they are a boy's talks. No story of a Japanese boy's life by a Japanese boy himself existed in America, he notes. Chapters give his birthplace, his grandfather, and the old-fashioned school. Kitchen, dinner, and food follow. Games, baths, evenings at home, and the theatre fill the middle. Wrestling, story-tellers, and an old castle crowd in. New Year's mochi-making and kite-flying close the year. Shigemi learned the alphabet only a few years before writing.
35543-my-little-boy:
My Little Boy is a book by Carl Ewald, translated from the Danish by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos. Scribner's Sons held the copyright in 1906 for this authorised translation. The book is a father's record of his small son's early life. It opens by saying the little boy is beginning to live. He makes his way over the paving stones, stumbling on knock-kneed legs. He looks at everything there is to look at. He bites at every apple, his due and forbidden alike.

He is not a pretty child, the father writes plainly. He is the more likely to grow into a fine lad for that. But he is charming, with a face that lights up suddenly. He has never yet bartered a kiss for barley sugar. The sketches catch a toddler's character in a tender, ironic voice.
35930-bevis-the-story-of-a-boy:
Richard Jefferies wrote Bevis, The Story of a Boy, in an 1882 London edition. Volume One opens at a farmhouse on a bright morning. A large wood case has just come to the house. Bevis runs for a chisel and a hammer to open it at once.

Bevis bruises his fingers in his haste to lift the lid. The case holds just a print of an old English fair. He claims the case as his own prize. He drags it to a shed and weighs what to make of it. A hut roof is his first plan. The tale stays close to a boy's work, play, and wild plans in the country.
36336-gabriel-conroy:
Gabriel Conroy is a novel of California by Bret Harte, in the Riverside edition of his works. Houghton, Mifflin and Company published this edition at Boston in 1882. The novel itself was copyrighted in 1875 by the American Publishing Company. 

Contents divide the tale into books with ominous chapter titles from the start. Book one, On the Threshold, runs from Without and Within to Gabriel himself in order. Chapters named Footprints, in which the footprints begin to fade, grow fainter, and are lost for ever close that book. Book two, After Five Years, opens at One Horse Gulch with Madame Devarges and Mrs Markle in its cast. The shape is plain: a party lost in the Sierra snow, a mystery of identity, and a return years later to the mining country where the secret works itself out.
36388-airship-andy-or-the-luck-of-a-brav:
Airship Andy, or The Luck of a Brave Boy, is a boys' novel by Frank V Webster. Cupples and Leon published it in New York in 1911. Andy Nelson works as a young chauffeur at Talbot's Automobile Garage in Princeville. In the first chapter he refuses to hand a customer's lost money to Gus Talbot. Gus is the owner's loafing son, and bluff fails on Andy.

Andy is poor, homeless, and friendless. He cannot even remember his parents. The chapter titles carry him from the garage to the aero field. He meets John Parks, the airship king, and learns to fly. Spying, an old leather pocketbook, and a stretch behind bars follow. The great race fills the climax chapter. Webster wrote a shelf of such books for boys. Honest pluck and a new machine lift Andy out of the garage for good.
36816-king-matthias-and-the-beggar-boy:
King Matthias and the Beggar Boy, adapted from the Hungarian of Baron Nicholas Josika by Selina Gaye, was published in 1902 by Nelson and Sons of London, Edinburgh, and New York. Gaye had written Ilka, the Captive Maiden before it. Nine chapters tell the tale, and a plate shows the king beckoning a Jewish man with the words, Come here, gossip Jew; there is nothing to fear.

Chapter one brings a dusty traveller, at the close of a gloomy autumn day, to Mr Samson's castle in one of the northern counties of Hungary. The castle defeats description: a square block on a height, with neither door nor window in any of its four sides, and an owner no outsider has ever seen. Miska the beggar boy, a robber's nest, a capture, prison, and the king's whim follow in the contents.
37296-samboe-or-the-african-boy:
Samboe, or the African Boy, came from Harvey and Darton of London in 1823, by the author of Twilight Hours Improved. The volume is dedicated, by his kind permission, to William Wilberforce, member of Parliament, in veneration of his virtues. Verses by Montgomery head the title page: bondage is winter, darkness, death, despair; freedom the sun and the sea.

The advertisement addresses young readers directly. The slave trade, it says, is little known to the rising generation, since Britain abolished it before many of them were born. Yet other nations still pursue it, and the tale is meant to stir young hearts against it.
37325-harry-milvaine-or-the-wanderings-o:
Harry Milvaine, or The Wanderings of a Wayward Boy, was written by Gordon Stables and published by Hodder and Stoughton of London. This edition is dated eighteen eighty-seven. Stables wrote sea and adventure tales for boys, and Harry is one of his restless young heroes.

The opening finds small Harry standing on an upturned stable bucket beside the water tank. He watches bright bubbles sail across the surface and makes a navy of them. The bubbles are ships of war, Harry is a king, and bursting bubbles mean victories and sinkings. Stables draws the child with patience: dark round eyes, a pale face, and an inventive mind. The subtitle promises wanderings, and the portrait of a boy who cannot sit still explains why.
37376-wang-the-ninth-the-story-of-a-chin:
Putnam Weale's Wang the Ninth, the story of a Chinese boy, was published by Dodd, Mead of New York in 1920, and dated from Peking in July 1919. Weale's earlier books on China stand listed at the front: Manchu and Muscovite, The Fight for the Republic in China, and Indiscreet Letters from Peking.

Wang was born a few years before the century's end in Ten Li Hamlet, ten Chinese miles from the imperial highway. He was the eighth child, and called the Ninth for that reason: eight joined to his surname would make a term of insult no Chinese could survive. At three, barely weaned, he was set on a creaking wheelbarrow and trundled into the unknown. Famine had fallen on the hamlet, his brothers and sisters leased or sold one by one, till he and his father were the last of the family left.
3785-in-the-reign-of-terror-the-adventur:
George Alfred Henty sends a Westminster schoolboy to France on the eve of the Revolution in this boys' tale. The boy's family debates the journey, weighing a long road among a people in upheaval. Soon he is caught in the Terror itself, with mad dogs, demon wolves, and gathering clouds as early warnings. Chapters carry him through the September massacres, the arrest of Marie, the shadow of Robespierre, and the drownings at Nantes.

Henty promises facts kept correct where the story needs them, save for the Nantes dates, which he owns he moved. The hero's courage lies in protecting friends rather than in battles, and the escape to England closes the book. Young readers who like history with adventure will find a brisk and stirring introduction to revolutionary France.
38027-autobiography-of-countess-tolstoy:
Sophie Andreevna Tolstoy wrote an Autobiography of Countess Tolstoy, translated by S S Koteliansky and Leonard Woolf, issued in New York by B W Huebsch in MCMXXII. The text was lately found and published in Russia in a new review, Nachala, edited by Vassili Spiridonov. His preface and notes come with the translation. Appendices print Tolstoy wills and an account of his going away. Tolstoy wife tells her own life.

The notes hold much material on Tolstoy not before open to English readers, the translators say. The question of Tolstoy going away and of his relations with his wife and family has stirred deep interest, they note. The autobiography runs from her girlhood and marriage through the long Yasnaya Polyana years. Her copying of War and Peace, the children, and the late quarrels over the will fill the tale. Readers get the marriage from the wife side, plain and defensive.
38572-love-sonnets-of-an-office-boy:
Samuel Ellsworth Kiser wrote Love Sonnets of an Office Boy. Forbes and Company issued it at Boston and Chicago in 1902. John T McCutcheon drew its pictures. The Chicago Record-Herald ran the verses first. Sonnet One opens in the office at once. Oh, if you only knowed how much I like, it starts.

The boy watches the typist's soft white fingers. The old man is away in that fond hour. Each key strike sounds like sweet music to him. You're twenty-five or six and I'm fourteen, he sighs. She calls him Willie when she notes him at all. He wishes for bundles of the old long green. He wishes himself twenty-eight or nine instead. The old man scolded her spelling in sonnet two. The boy dented his hat in spite for that. Comic sonnets in office slang gave newspaper readers a daily grin at young love's hopeless arithmetic.
38619-a-terrible-tomboy:
Angela Brazil wrote A Terrible Tomboy, a story for girls, here in a new edition with illustrations in colour by N Tenison. Henry Frowde and Hodder and Stoughton in London issued the book in nineteen fifteen. Brazil had earlier written Fairy Plays for Children. Twenty four chapters fill the book. Peggy is the tomboy heroine, and chapter one is Peggy at Home.

Birds Nesting, The Black Puppy, and A Stormy Day open the fun. Concerning Lilian, Sunday, and Maud Middleton Party follow. The Holidays, A Mountain Walk, and On the Moors fill the middle. A New Friend, In the Rectory Garden, and The Smugglers Cave bring fresh turns. Lilian Housekeeping and The Beginning of a Shadow deepen the tale. Dame Eleanor Ghost, Play Acting, and Peggy at War close it. Girls get school, moors, and mischief in bright prose.
39757-half-hours-with-jimmieboy:
Half-Hours with Jimmieboy is a children's story book by John Kendrick Bangs. Bangs also wrote the Tiddledywink Tales. Russell and Son published it in New York in 1893. Five illustrators, including Peter Newell, drew for the volume. Bangs dedicated the book to his son Francis Hyde Bangs. Thanks are given to Harper for leave to reprint several stories. The contents list sixteen tales of a small boy's adventures.

Christmas Eve at Jimmieboy's opens the collection. A dwarf, a dude giant, and a subterranean mutiny follow. Jimmieboy visits a library, makes a snowman, and meets Jack Frost. A comet, fireworks, and a blank book give other adventures. The first tale begins on a long and trying December day. Christmas Eve is hard for children waiting, the narrator observes. The stories blend household fun with fairy tale invention.
39871-bikey-the-skicycle-and-other-tales:
Bikey the Skicycle and Other Tales of Jimmieboy is a children's book by John Kendrick Bangs. Riggs published it in New York in 1902. Peter Newell illustrated the tales in this volume. Bangs also wrote Mr Munchausen and House Boat on the Styx. The contents list twelve tales of Jimmieboy's adventures. Bikey the Skicycle fills the first and longest place. The Imp of the Telephone follows as the second tale. Caught in Toy Town and Totherwayville, the Animal Town come next.

An Electrical Error and In the Brownie's House continue the wonders. Jimmieboy and Something and his fireworks give later tales. High-Jinks in the Barn and Jimmieboy's Valentine turn homely. The Magic Sled and The Stupid Little Apple Tree close the list. A frontispiece shows a stranger being particular at a door. The tales mix new machines with fairy tale mischief.
40260-the-last-days-of-tolstoy:
Vladimir Tchertkoff, Tolstoy's friend and fellow worker, wrote the story of the great man's flight from home. Nathalie Duddington turned it into English, and Heinemann of London published it in 1922. The first part asks why Tolstoy did not leave his home for so long.

Tchertkoff answers that the step had to feel needful before Tolstoy could take it. Staying was the harder path, and his love for his wife held him. The second part tells why he went at last. Life at Yasnaya Polyana had grown rich around a man who preached plain living. The long fight over his will, and his giving up of the rights in his books, sits at the centre. The last chapters trace the night of the going away.
43142-a-london-baby-the-story-of-king-ro:
A London Baby, the story of King Roy, is a tale by Meade, put out at London in a print of eighteen eighty two. It starts with a first word in the form of a fore tale. The teller first saw King Roy on a fair eve of the warm time near a great park of the town. It was the rest day of the week, and a light, sweet wind just eased the heat.

In a sport mood that wind caught the small soft cap of the babe and threw it past his curls. Then came a race, a scrum, and a laugh, in which the teller, a strange hand to his small high rank, took part. That sport led her to mark him with more care.
43390-the-factory-boy:
The Factory Boy is a children's story by Aunt Hattie, printed at Boston by Henry Young and Company. The copyright was entered in 1867. Her motto text is David's: trust in the Lord and do good, and verily thou shalt be fed. The volumes are inscribed to the children of her beloved nephew, a clergyman.

The hero is Johnny, a poor factory child. The first chapter, The Silver Dollar, opens on a frosty December morning. His mother offers him a cup of porridge before work. He hurries away, for the factory bell is ringing and he must not be late. His shoes are much too large, their heels so worn that he must shuffle to keep them on. Aunt Hattie wrote Sunday school fiction against child labour, with the mill bell as its villain.
43905-south-from-hudson-bay-an-adventure:
South from Hudson Bay is an adventure and mystery story for boys by Brill, published in 1932. The publisher was Cupples and Leon of New York. The tale is set in the fur-trade north of Canada. A frontispiece shows a boat reaching a crowded landing. The contents list runs to more than thirty-eight chapters. Fort York and the Selkirk Colony stand early in the tale.

The story follows a journey south from the bay. Rival fur traders clash along the route. The travellers toil up stream to Norway House. Pemmican goes missing, and hunger and cold set in. Carts carry the party to Pembina for Christmas. Sioux, buffalo hunters, and a painted skull crowd the later chapters. Brill wrote a shelf of such tales for boys. The Secret Cache and The Island of Yellow Sands are its mates.
44970-the-recollections-of-a-drummer-boy:
The Recollections of a Drummer Boy is a Civil War memoir by Harry Kieffer, a Union veteran. Kieffer served in the One Hundred and Fiftieth Regiment of Pennsylvania Volunteers. Osgood published the book at Boston in eighteen eighty three, with pictures. Its motto is a Latin line from Virgil's Aeneid about remembering past days.

The sketches first ran in Saint Nicholas, a magazine for the young, years before. Editors and readers pressed Kieffer for more of the same kind of writing. He revised and enlarged them into one connected story of a soldier's life. The arc runs from enlistment to muster out, through camp and field in turn. He wrote for the soldiers' children and for the veterans themselves alike. The volume is inscribed to the officers and men of his old regiment.
45022-bernard-brooks-adventures-the-expe:
Horatio Alger wrote this tale of a plucky boy for Burt of New York, who printed it in 1903. Bernard Brooks's Adventures opens in a schoolroom quarrel. You're a bad lot, Bernard Brooks, says Mr Snowdon; I never knew a worse boy.

Thank you for the compliment, Mr Snowdon, the boy fires back. And wuss, he adds, is hardly correct English. Bernard stands fifteen, tall as most boys of seventeen. His bold manner comes out for those he counts as foes. To a friend he is devoted; to a kind master, loyal. Snowdon, a stooping man of sixty who runs a cheap private school, is no friend. Alger's old war — pluck against spite — starts hot.
45156-sinopah-the-indian-boy:
Sinopah, the Indian Boy, by James Willard Schultz, who signs also his Blackfoot name Apikuni, was copyrighted in 1913 and published by Houghton Mifflin. Drawings by Boyd Smith picture the tale. Eleven chapters follow Sinopah from his naming through an escape from buffalo, the buffalo trap, his first bow, and tracking a mountain lion, to his joining the Mosquito Society.

Chapter one tells that Sinopah grew up to be the great chief Pitamakan, the Running Eagle. Schultz knew Pitamakan well, and his white partner Thomas Fox too. Both men told him of their boyhood days, so the story claims to be true. Sinopah was born in the time of the buffalo, in a great Blackfoot camp on the Two Medicine River, on a warm June day.
47353-tolstoy:
L Winstanley, lecturer in English at the University College of Wales, wrote Tolstoy, a short life and study, issued in London by T C and E C Jack. Winstanley gave the book to her beloved friend Anna Brodsky. Eight chapters and a bibliography fill the volume. Chapter one treats Tolstoy contemporaries. The rise of Russian authors is her opening theme.

The most striking literary phenomenon of the nineteenth century is the rise into power of Russian authors, she opens. Fifty years ago Russian literature was practically unknown to Western Europe, she says. Even Carlyle spoke of the great silent Russians who had produced nothing articulate as yet, she notes. In less than thirty years Russian literature was recognized as a world power, she adds. Chapters then treat the life, War and Peace, and Anna Karénina. My Confession and Resurrection close the study.
479-little-lord-fauntleroy:
Frances Hodgson Burnett tells of Cedric Errol, a kind American boy who learns he is heir to an English earldom, in this beloved children's novel. Cedric lives in New York with his widowed mother, loved by shopkeepers and friends. When his stern grandfather summons him to England, Cedric's goodness begins to melt the old earl's pride.

Burnett writes with warmth and gentle humor, letting a child's plain kindness shame adult greed. Velvet suits and curls made Fauntleroy a fashion craze in his day. The book endures as a sweet tale of innocence softening rank, and of a boy who stays himself in a castle.
48291-strange-stories-of-the-great-valle:
Strange Stories of the Great Valley is a boys tale of a young first settler, by Grosvenor. Prints fill its form. It came out at New York and London. Its rights were set in law in the last years of the great war. A print at its front shows a shout of good luck. The shouter is a lad nick named for his beard.

A note tells how its print form was set. Slant text stands by marks in it. Raised signs for small print show by a wedge mark. Its tales roam the great vale of the west in the first years. Hunts, red men, and lost trails fill them. The deeds by which a lad of the log house age grew to a man fill them as well.
48666-the-sepoy:
Edmund Candler wrote this account of the Indian soldier classes in 1919. John Murray printed the book in London that year. Contents treat each class in turn, from the Gurkha onward. Photos show a Sikh, a Pathan piper band, and a Jat sowar.

The Sikh, Punjabi Mussalman, Pathan, Dogra, and Mahratta follow the Gurkha. Jat, Rajput and Brahman, Garhwali, Khattak, and Hazara come next. Mer, Ranghar, Meena, Jharwa, and Drabi fill the later chapters. A Santal Labour Corps and the Indian follower close the survey. Candler opens by owning that Gurkha and Sikh fame is well deserved indeed.
49435-tolstoy:
Rolland, author of Jean Christophe, wrote this life of Tolstoy for Fisher Unwin in 1911, in Miall's translation. The life had ended, and Rolland reads it. Our instinct, he begins, was conscious then of what reason must prove today. The life has remained the same from beginning to end, he argues, in spite of the barriers critics raise.

There is no unity of ideas in Tolstoy, only the persistence of the same elements, more often enemies than allies. The contents follow the life: childhood, the army, the tales of the Caucasus, and Sebastopol. Family happiness, marriage, and Anna Karenin lead to the crisis. Art and conscience, the theories of art and music, and Resurrection fill the later chapters. Religion and politics and old age close the book. In Tolstoy, Rolland concludes, life and art are one, and the journal he kept lets us read his conscience.
50098-the-war-history-of-the-4th-battali:
War History of the 4th Battalion, the London Regiment (Royal Fusiliers), 1914 to 1919, is a unit history by Captain Grimwade. The battalion headquarters at Shaftesbury Avenue in London published the book in 1922. Grimwade served in the battalion whose record he compiles here for its men. 

The history is dedicated to the memory of Colonel Wilde, who commanded the battalion from 1890 to 1903. Wilde had compiled its historical records from 1643 to 1908 before the war. Contents open with mobilisation and the departure overseas of the battalion in 1914. Chapter two treats the first line battalion in Malta and the formation of a second line battalion at home. Battalion histories like this one, written by officers for survivors and families, are the ground level record of the Great War. They name the drafts, marches, and actions that grand strategy passes over in silence.
50246-running-to-waste-the-story-of-a-to:
George M Baker wrote a girls' story entered for copyright in 1874, as part of the Maidenhood Series. Becky Sleeper sits on a wall that bounds Captain Thompson's orchard, where she has no business to be. Her brother Teddy drops apples into her apron from the tree above. The first chapter is titled Stolen Sweets.

Baker dedicated the book to a patient invalid friend who said the tale lightened her weary hours. Chapters follow fallen fortunes, Becky's charity, and her last frolic. A chapter called Becky's New Birth marks a turn. Teddy dines out, Delia's ship comes in, and a chapter set two years after closes the story.
50702-venus-boy:
Venus Boy is a children's science fiction novel by Lee Sutton, published in New York in 1955. Richard Floethe illustrated the book. Its hero is a twelve-year-old boy named Virgil Dare Watson, called Johnny.

Johnny was the first human being born on Venus, named after Virginia Dare, the first pioneer child born in North America. For a long time he was the only child on the planet. His best friend is Baba, a Venusian jewel bear who rides on his shoulder. The opening pages describe the fifty-foot statue of the boy and the bear above the colony of New Plymouth. It calls the pair the planet's greatest hero and his companion. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
50848-soldier-boy:
Michael Shaara wrote Soldier Boy, a science fiction story printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in July 1953, with pictures by Emsh. A Scandinavian legend opens it. In a great cave in the northland, by an everburning fire, the Warrior sleeps through a thousand years of peace. Yet the people will summon him again when they are sore in need.

The story moves to a colony world. On a freezing morning, with snow on the wind, an army ship lands near the settlement. The colonists grumble and stay indoors; they want no soldiers here. A tall, frail-looking man steps out and waits stiffly, his face turned from the wind. The magazine's tag line gives the theme: it is one thing to laugh at a man whose job seems outdated, and another to depend on him when it suddenly is not.
5111-the-real-diary-of-a-real-boy:
Henry A. Shute's book presents itself as a boy's diary, found years later in a salt-box fitted with leather hinges in his father's shed chamber. The entries record school, pranks, friendships, and small-town life with the spelling, boasts. Earnestness marks every entry, and a later introduction looks back on them thirty years on.

The diary's humour lies in its honesty: the writer takes himself very seriously while the reader sees the comedy. It offers a warm, funny portrait of American boyhood around the turn of the century. It has lasted as a small classic of humour precisely because its hero never knows how funny he is.
52559-the-ballad-of-ensign-joy:
Ernest William Hornung wrote The Ballad of Ensign Joy, a long poem in verse published by Dutton and Company in 1917. Its hero is a young English officer of the Special Reserves, stuck on coast defence duty and eager to be sent overseas. He falls in with Ermyntrude, a prim and pretty girl who holds him at arm's length.

The poem follows Joy from training camps to the front in France. His cheerful letters home, full of jokes about the fighting, pain her even as her friends laugh at them. Hornung mixes light romance with the grim facts of the First World War. The ballad honors the young men who rushed to serve, while showing the gap between home-front talk and life under fire.
53345-dan-the-newsboy:
Dan, the Newsboy is a story for boys by Horatio Alger, with copyright in 1893 at New York. Alger also wrote The Train Boy and Tony the Hero, and his name stood for tales of poor boys rising by pluck and honesty. The contents run to forty-two chapters, and the tale opens with Dan calling his papers on a city street.

Dan cries the Evening Telegram, one left, going for two cents and worth double the money. A gentleman pauses at the steps of the Astor House, struck by the boy's businesslike tone. From there the heads promise loans, thefts found out, a mysterious lady named Althea, a burglary, and a kidnapping, before Dan is adopted at the close.
54270-the-human-boy:
Eden Phillpotts wrote these schoolboy tales of the human boy at Merivale. Harper printed the book in New York and London in 1900. Phillpotts gives it to Phillpotts Minor in fraternal regard and memory. Contents open with the artfulness of Steggles in first place.

A wing dormitory protest and Freckles and Frenchy follow the opener. Corkey Minimus, a piebald rat, and Browne and Bradwell appear. Gideon front tooth, a chemistry class, and a howler fill middle. Nubby Tomkins roasts chestnuts and fears death from a chest cold. A half sovereign and a set of buckeneers fill the final tales of school life.
54350-jed-the-poorhouse-boy:
Jed, the Poorhouse Boy, is a novel by Horatio Alger, the famed writer of boys' tales of pluck and luck. Winston published it at Philadelphia with an 1899 copyright. Jed is first seen splitting wood, his axe paused above him, turning toward a thin, sharp faced woman at the side door. Well, what's wanted, he asks.

The contents name his keepers, Mr and Mrs Fogson, and the Scranton poorhouse where he lives. An exciting contest, an ally secured, and Fogson's mistake build toward Jed leaving the poorhouse. He reaches Duncan, makes his first appearance on the stage, and baffles Percy Dixon. Fogson pursues, Jed is discharged, and his prospects look poor. Then New York, two calls, a startling discovery, and days without a penny follow. This late tale sends its hero through the theatre to fortune.
54604-being-a-boy:
Charles Dudley Warner wrote of being a boy in a book first printed in 1877 and reissued at Boston and New York in 1897 with photographs by Clifton Johnson. Fishing on the swimming rock fronts the volume. Being a boy opens the chapters, then the boy as a farmer and the delights of farming. No farming without a boy comes fourth.

The boy's Sunday, the grindstone of life, fiction and sentiment, and the coming of Thanksgiving follow. The season of pumpkin pie, first sight of the world, home inventions, and the lonely farm house fill the middle. John's first party, the sugar camp, the heart of New England, and war close the set. One of the best things in the world to be is a boy, Warner begins. It needs no experience, though it takes practice to be a good one.
55000-mark-manning-s-mission-the-story-o:
Horatio Alger wrote a boys' novel about Mark Manning, a lad who works in a shoe factory. This copy was issued in New York in 1905, with five page plates by Watson Davis. The tale opens with two boys bound for the Pecasset woods with guns on their shoulders.

Mark meets a hermit who counts out gold and speaks of three hundred and fifty dollars left. A sly rival, Lyman Taylor, hunts for that gold and plots against the boy. Chapters bring a lost job, a trip to New York, and a charge laid on Mark that gives the book its name. As in most Alger tales, grit and good conduct win out at last.
56481-peanut-the-story-of-a-boy:
Albert Bigelow Paine, biographer of Mark Twain, wrote the story of a boy nicknamed Peanut, issued in 1913. A list of his books gives the tale's price as fifty cents. The opening scene is grim for a boy's book: a small clearing about a grave in the hills.

Blackened stumps mark the spot, and a two-inch headboard, weathered by a year of sun and rain, is near lost in bushes. Stage drivers point it out as the last hangout of Blazer Sam, who died with his boots on. Travellers climb for a closer look at the two cuss-words of his epitaph. From that grave the boy's story is told backward and forward.
56783-thrills-of-a-bell-boy:
Samuel Ellsworth Kiser wrote Thrills of a Bell Boy, comic verse first copyrighted in 1904 and printed at Chicago in 1906. McCutcheon drew the pictures. Kiser had written Love Sonnets of an Office Boy in the same vein.

A hotel bell boy tells his tales in slangy sonnets. A call from room seven-forty-eight brings ice for Miss Le Claire, star of Mrs Middleton's Regret, who draws a hundred dollars. He dreams of her dude rival and of wearing a plug hat himself. Later pieces mock the traveling men who swagger in, make eyes at the telegraph girl, and act as though they had come to buy the town.
57497-the-land-of-joy:
A college novel by Ralph Henry Barbour. Doubleday, Page and Company published it at New York in 1903. Twenty-six chapters follow John North and his friends. Their stage is Harvard, and their time is one college year. The title quotes a verse by Butler. Youth walks onward in it, with the land of joy before his eyes.

The first chapter brings North back to Cambridge in late September. His study on Dunster Street stands shuttered and stifling. He throws the windows up and sorts the clutter of class day. Barbour wrote many school and college stories. This one promises friendship, sport, and undergraduate scrapes seen from inside a student's rooms.
5778-try-and-trust-or-abner-holden-s-bou:
Horatio Alger tells the story of Abner Holden's bound boy in Try and Trust, opening around a breakfast table. Benjamin Stanton tells his wife he had a letter from Ohio the day before, from his sister Margaret, who moved there with her husband ten years earlier. From that domestic opening, the novel follows a bound boy's struggle for fair treatment, honest work, and a chance to rise.

Readers meet Alger's familiar pattern with fresh feeling: a young hero, hard masters, kind friends, and steady effort rewarded. The book favors clear morals and brisk incident over fine psychology, which is its charm for young readers. It offers a plain, encouraging tale of trust earned and kept, in the world of farms, shops, and small-town bargains.
58164-doodles-the-sunshine-boy:
Doodles, the Sunshine Boy, is a tale for the young by Emma Dowd. Prints by Maria Kirk dress the text in colour and line. Past tales by the same hand tell of Polly and her hospital kin. The book came out in Boston in the year nineteen fifteen.

Doodles keeps joy in hard days, and one plate shows him glad in song. The tag on the cover claims he is never lone while he can sing. Home and school scenes in plain talk shape the small warm tale. The book aims to lift young hearts that face pain or loss. Soft faith and pluck mark its place on the gift shelf.
58165-when-you-were-a-boy:
Edwin L Sabin wrote When You Were a Boy, sketches of boyhood told to the grown reader. The Baker and Taylor Company issued the book in New York in October nineteen hundred five. Frederic Dorr Steele drew the pictures. Parts first ran in the Century Magazine and other monthlies.

Fat Day captains the North Stars in the match game that opens it. He owns the ball, so none dare cross his claim. You, the reader as boy, plays center field on his nine. Billy Lunt catches, a post too sore for any rival. School, chums, the circus, and a runaway fill the next scenes. Fishing, swimming, and a Sunday school picnic crowd the warm year. The old muzzle loader and a boy’s first loves close the set. Sabin writes each sketch as your own lost days come back.
58262-captain-john-s-adventures-or-the-s: Captain John Adventures is a tale for the young, sold as one of a set of sixpenny books from Edinburgh and London. Its short title calls it the story of a boy with no father. The set that held it was made for young readers at a low price. Names in that set tell of orphans, lame girls, and waifs in like straits.
58743-little-boy:
Harry Neal wrote a short tale printed in Worlds of If in October 1954. A grim motto heads it: the beast in man at times asserts itself with savage force. Even children turn into snarling little beasts, it says. Yet in childhood, laughter is not buried deep.

Steven, eleven years old, drops over the Central Park wall and flattens to the ground. He has forgotten his own name. His face is sunburned, bitter and filthy, his clothes mere rags. Knife in hand, he watches like a young wolf, head down and eyes up. Ruined blocks line the street behind him, and no one stirs in the park below.
59195-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of Leon Tolstoy is a finding aid compiled by David Widger. In substance it is a map of his shelf: every volume's contents without opening each file. The master list runs from The Forged Coupon to War and Peace and the early trilogy.

Anna Karenina's eight parts and Resurrection's chapter list let a reader trace the novels' shape. Plays, fables for children, tales, essays on religion and art, the journal, and the late pamphlets all appear with their tables. Translations are credited where the edition names them. For readers of the free Gutenberg texts, the index is the quickest way to find a story or check a chapter.
59540-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
An index of the Project Gutenberg works of John McElroy guides readers to his books. David Widger compiled the index for the online set of his writings. Andersonville heads the list, his famed story of rebel military prisons. Uncle Daniel, the Struggle for Missouri, and the Red Acorn follow. Six books of the Si Klegg tales stand listed in their order.

The Economic Functions of Vice closes the contents list of the index. Andersonville tells fifteen months as a guest of the Southern Confederacy. A private soldier's life in Richmond, Savannah, Millen, and Florence fills it. Chapters run from a strange land in the Appalachians to surrender. Living off the enemy and camp cookery fill the early war chapters. Cold, hunger, and sad reflection follow the reaction after battle there. The index lets a reader open any chapter of any book listed.
60939-superjoemulloy:
Scott Grenville wrote a sharp science fiction tale for Worlds of If in November 1960. Joe Mulloy is a perfect man, and the only road past his perfection leads to the title the tale gives him. Joe lounges in a lush office lined with mirrors, even on the floor and ceiling. He shapes his famous sneer with his hands and admires it from every side.

That sneer ruled his youth. It enraged his father, saddened his mother, and drove his teachers to tears. He quit homework at eight, yet the schools passed him on to be rid of him. At fifteen the local board ended his schooling for good. His father threw him out of the house. Three days later the memory of that sneer drove the man to shoot himself. Joe, for all his show of idleness, works hard at his own trade. He is a builder of robots.
60970-ben-bruce-scenes-in-the-life-of-a-:
Horatio Alger wrote scenes in the life of a Bowery newsboy, copyrighted in 1892 and reissued at New York in 1901 with illustrations. Ben Bruce, bright-faced and fearless, opens under the thumb of his stepfather Jacob Winter, a weather-beaten man whose heavy frown and stern voice carry danger signals the boy reads at once.

Forty chapters carry Ben far beyond the Bowery: witness to an explosion, a midnight call, a disappointed burglar, and a sudden determination. He arrives in Boston, becomes a hero, dines in Mt Vernon Street, gets employment, makes his début on the stage, and meets with strange prosperity. Titled friends and a journey to Geneva widen the close. The Alger ladder, climbed at full speed, is the story.
62045-leo-tolstoy:
Leo Tolstoy is a portrait volume with text by Chesterton, Perris, and others. Copp Clark issued it at Toronto, with Hodder and Stoughton in London. A frontispiece shows Tolstoy, and a long list of plates maps his life in pictures.

The plates show Tolstoy as an officer, as a student, and on his bicycle at Yasnaya Polyana. His country home, its gateway, and the tree of the poor all appear. Portraits by Repin, a page of his manuscript, and a postcard from his 1898 literary jubilee fill the set. The opening essay warns that the full measure of the man is not found in his novels alone. Nor do his ethical views, fine as they are, give the whole of his character and influence.
62935-mewanee-the-little-indian-boy:
Belle Wiley, a teacher of methods at the Rochester training school, wrote this 1912 story book for young readers, with pictures by Charles Hubbard. Mewanee is a brave little Indian boy living in a North American forest. His father is chief of the tribe, and Mewanee is proud to be the chief's son. His baby brother swings in a linden-bark cradle lined with soft rushes, tied in with deer sinews.

Left watching the baby, Mewanee dashes after a hare and forgets him, chasing it in and out among the trees. The chapters go on through the home, the hunt, the enemy, and the friendly tribe. A council, time in the forest, a sacrifice, and a fast follow, ending with a new home. Silver, Burdett published the book at Boston, New York, and Chicago for school and home reading.
62956-jed-s-boy: Jed's Boy is a boys' tale of the Civil War, issued at New York by Thomas Y Crowell Company. The hosted copy opens with the publisher's list of Warren Lee Goss's Civil War stories for boys, among them In the Navy, Tom Clifton, Jack Alden, and Jed. The book's frontispiece follows, with a line from its first page: I gripped my nerve and shut my teeth; could I reach a place of safety? No title page or text stands in the head.
63182-pat-the-lighthouse-boy:
E Everett-Green tells a boy's sea tale in Pat, the Lighthouse Boy, issued by Ward and Drummond of New York. The contents move from Lone Rock Lighthouse through fog and storm and a terrible night to Jim's exploit and a chapter called The Little Prince. A plate asks where Jim will go when they take him ashore.

Pat arrives at the lighthouse with his mother, fresh from a crowded alley in a fishing town, and thinks he has gone straight to heaven. He is a frail little fellow who has just been very ill. His Irish mother, who has lost kin to the sea, answers more soberly.
65080-dick-rodney-or-the-adventures-of-a:
James Grant's sea story follows an Eton boy into every peril the ocean can offer. Lippincott published it at Philadelphia. Dick Rodney had been an oppidan at Eton, high in favor with his house master and the Vice Provost. But he spent his hours on boxing gloves, fencing foils, cricket, and rowing. Books of wild adventure, from Defoe to the Railway Library, filled him with longings no regatta could satisfy.

The contents promise the rest. Dick ships under Captain Zeervogel, drifts from the Eugenie, and rides a hurricane to the Fortunate Isles. Antonio El Cubano is unmasked, Tom is tattooed, and the crew is cast away on the Island of Alphonso. Later come a mutiny, a waterlogged vessel, the old Spanish ship San Ildefonso, and a valley of diamonds off Africa. Sangre por sangre, blood for blood, is one chapter's title and the voyage's motto.
658-the-fall-of-troy:
Quintus Smyrnaeus, a Greek poet of Smyrna from about the fourth century, continues Homer's tale in this epic, here in A. S. Way's 1913 translation. The Iliad ends with Hector's burial; Quintus takes up the story from Penthesileia, queen of the Amazons, through Memnon, Achilles' death, the arms of Achilles, the Wooden Horse, and Troy's sack.

Way's verse keeps Homer's ring and music in English, with notes on the Cyclic poets whose works are lost. Fourteen books carry the war to its fiery end. The poem serves as the great sequel to the Iliad, where a later Greek poet completes what Homer left unsung.
65945-the-toy:
The Toy is a short star tale by Kris Neville from a December nineteen fifty two pulp. Neju leads his folk in a night creep on a fenced fort of the God men. He hates not the God men but the steel fiends they use to slay his tribe. Prayers to the Old Gods for aid frame his grim march. Grass blades sting and stones bruise the band as they crawl in moon light.

A strange front talk shows a child beg to leave a gift for a folk. A toy of hers might serve them some day, she pleads with her dam. Two guards pace the wall walk in clock true turns as the band nears. The wall is built of close set trunks shorn of limbs. The tale plays on what high craft gifts mean to a low craft folk.
66248-the-texas-hawks-or-the-strange-dec:
Jos E Badger Jr wrote The Texas Hawks, or The Strange Decoy, issued by Beadle and Adams at New York. The number is dated September 30, 1876, though the tale was entered for copyright in 1872. Eleven chapters fill it. The strange rider opens, and the lottery of death follows. A midnight conflict and the Baranca mystery come next. The maiden's peril and the lost trail raise the stakes.

On guard, at bay, and a strange proposal lead to the clew and a double surprise. The tale opens at a hunting party's bivouac. Half a score of hunters in blood-stained clothes rest around a crackling fire. Buffalo and deer meat hangs from the trees, and the horses graze close by, still wet with sweat. Two young men argue over a story one calls a sheer hoax.
67723-whistler-or-the-manly-boy:
Whistler, or The Manly Boy, is a moral tale for boys by Walter Aimwell. Gould and Lincoln published it at Boston in 1857. The book belongs to the Aimwell Stories. Each volume of that series stands complete alone. Illustrations accompany the text. A forest picnic is pictured in front.

A preface states the book's object directly. It portrays the character of the manly boy. Such a character inspires love and esteem when genuine. A lad may stay a real boy in tastes and feelings. Yet he may show true manliness in spirit and conduct. The series' advertisement explains the method. Quiet scenes of everyday life carry the lessons. Home, school, and playground supply the incidents. Startling adventures are deliberately avoided.
68127-stories-from-the-iliad-or-the-sieg:
Stories from the Iliad is a child form of the great Greek war poem, told by Jeanie Lang. Plates by a famed drawn hand fill it. Lang thanks three named men for their dress of the poem, of which she made free use. A front note says she made the book first for two Greek boys, who would soon read the tales in their own tongue.

Parts tell what led to the siege, how the two Greek chiefs fell out, and the fight of the two foe leads. A queen and a great wife, a talk past the slain, and a plea to the swift chief take parts. The death of the chiefs dear friend and his wake to wrath close the list shown. Lang holds such brave deeds must swell the hearts of boys of all lands.
68521-through-the-mill-the-life-of-a-mil:
Through the Mill, the life of a mill-boy, is an autobiography by Al Priddy, printed at Boston in 1911. A note at the front calls it a frank, real, and calm account written by a mill-boy who lived the experiences of the book. So far as could be found, it says, this was the first such autobiography printed in English.

The book first appeared in the Outlook and was then rewritten with new chapters. Its chapter titles tell the story in glimpses: fish, wrangles, and beer; dripping potatoes and diplomatic charity; schoolmates teaching the boy American. One chapter heads: I cannot become a President, but I can go to the dumping grounds. The verses at the front, from Elizabeth Barrett Browning, tell of iron wheels grinding life down while children's souls spin blindly in the dark. Priddy's book is a first-hand record of child labour in the mills.
69405-bolo-the-cave-boy:
Katherine Atherton Grimes tells a stone age tale in Bolo the Cave Boy, printed at Dansville, New York, with copyright in 1915. The Owen Publishing Company made the book, number 256 of the Instructor Literature Series. Wilson draws the plates.

Chapter one is how Bolo got his dinner. Bolo crept carefully through the tall grass, the tale starts. In one brown hand he parted the stalks before him. In the other he carried a noose made from a slender willow withe. His bright, black eyes peered about at every step. Ahead, a small gray rabbit hopped slowly along, stopping to nibble tender young grass. Bolo was hungry, and a little rabbit would make him a good dinner. The throw is foiled when a second boy breaks through the grass.
70289-corduroy:
Ruth Comfort Mitchell wrote Corduroy, a novel published by Appleton and Company in 1923. Mitchell had earlier written Play the Game and Jane Journeys On. Her heroine is Virginia Valdés McVeagh, called Ginger, a young woman of twenty-two who runs a cattle ranch in California with the help of vaqueros and an old mayordomo.

Ginger's father is dead, and her brother Aleck, her closest pal, was killed on the last day of fighting in the Great War. She has always sorted men into equals and inferiors, and mastered both. Then Dean Wolcott comes at Christmas, framed in mystery and grief. He brings word of her dead brother and a stained, crumpled letter in Aleck's own hand. The ranch romance turns on that letter.
70572-bomba-the-jungle-boy:
Roy Rockwood's Bomba the Jungle Boy, or The Old Naturalist's Secret, was published in New York by Cupples and Leon, with a copyright of 1926. The frontispiece shows Bomba bringing a paddle down with all his force. Cupples and Leon also list the later Bomba books and Rockwood's Great Marvel, Speedwell Boys and Dave Dashaway series.

The first chapter halts Bomba in the densest part of a gigantic jungle, alert to some sound beneath the parrots and monkeys. The contents promise a stealthy foe, a puma's den and a siege of terror. Vampires attack, a cloud of vultures gathers, and Bomba fights in the folds of a boa constrictor before a battle royal at the water hole.
71323-roy:
Agnes Giberne wrote Roy, a tale in the days of Sir John Moore, published in London in 1901. Verses by Norman Macleod open the book, recalling the retreat to Corunna and the night the general was buried. Giberne had earlier written Coulyng Castle and a tale of the days of James the Second.

The story begins with a trip to Paris in 1803, when Britain and France slid back into war. Chapters follow prisoners of war, a threatened invasion, and orders that move Roy from Verdun to Valenciennes and Bitche. Moore's army in Spain stands behind the tale. Giberne mixes a young hero's fortunes with real events of the Napoleonic wars, writing history as adventure for general readers.
72101-the-white-indian-boy:
The White Indian Boy, the story of Uncle Nick among the Shoshones, is a pioneer memoir by E N Wilson, revised and edited by Howard R Driggs. The World Book Company printed it at Yonkers in 1922 in the Pioneer Life Series. F N Wilson drew the illustrations. A picture shows Shoshone Falls of the Snake River, in the land of Washakie's tribe.

The foreword notes that the men and women who played a part in the conquest and settlement of the Great West grow fewer year by year. To put a pioneer's recollections into permanent form is a contribution to history. Wilson's cabin stands on Fish Creek at Wilson, Wyoming, below the Teton Mountains, on the road to Yellowstone by way of Jackson's Hole. As a boy he lived among the Shoshones, and his record shows the courage and hardihood of the settlers.
72119-deadly-decoy:
Clyde Mitchell plots an assassination in Deadly Decoy, from the February 1957 issue of Amazing Stories. The head blurb asks a hard question: would you say present day Secret Service men have a tough job protecting the President? As time goes on it will get tougher, it warns, and here is about as tricky a method of liquidation as we have ever come across.

The tale opens in a guarded office. A Damakoi visitor thanks the narrator for permission to come. The narrator glances at the instruments on a hidden desk panel. Across from him sits a member of the most fanatically dangerous race in the Galaxy. Every detector shows the blue skinned being harmless, which does not necessarily mean anything. Holdreth Khain of Damak may have something else up his sleeve.
73300-a-little-swiss-boy:
A Little Swiss Boy is a tale for the young by Johanna Spyri. Her famed book of the hills maid is named on the title leaf. More of her tales for the young are named there as well. Coumbe made the English form of this book. Frances Brundage made its plates. It was put out in the west in nineteen twenty six.

The list of parts runs to one part past ten. In Leuk heads the tale, and in the field comes next. Strange turns, a start and a come, and a life past home fill the first run. Still more high up the hill, still more song, and more strange turns stand past them. New shocks, not for one boy a lone, old friends and new life, and the old song once more close the book.
75624-the-house-of-joy:
Laurence Housman wrote eight fairy tales in a book printed at London in 1895. The prince with the nine sorrows opens the set. The luck of the roses and the white king follow. The tale of the herons and Syringa fill the middle.

The traveller's shoes, the moon flower, and happy returns close the book. The first tale opens with a verse of eight white pea hens at a gate. A king's son is born, and his queen mother gives him to a forester's wife to nurse. The two babes feed as twins. Then the queen dreams him dead at twenty, a wound over his heart, his foster sister crowned beside him. The house fairy is called, and the queen forbids the child's death.
75999-a-journey-of-joy:
A Journey of Joy, by Amy E Blanchard, was printed by Dana Estes at Boston, with a copyright of 1908 and art by L J Bridgman. Blanchard gives the tale to her niece May, whose good cheer lit the true trip it rests on. It opens at dusk in late November, with two women at a dim lawn. The elder drops the news: she goes to Italy, and not alone. Sidney goes with her, to the girl's mock wrath.
